USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue negotiating from a position of leverage without introducing new escalatory measures. Hold existing tariffs as bargaining chips, press hard on the enforcement mechanism and structural IP/tech-transfer reforms, and be willing to extend the timeline rather than rush a weak deal. Do not raise List 3 to 25% yet — the threat of escalation is more valuable than executing it while talks are progressing.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE:

THREAT SCORE (-0.35): The US holds meaningful leverage in this dispute. China's economy is materially weaker than ours: manufacturing PMI has been contracting for two consecutive months (official 49.4-49.5, Caixin 48.3 in Jan 2019), export orders shrinking for 7+ months, and GDP growth forecast to slow to 6.2% — the weakest in nearly 30 years. The end of front-loading effects means China's export sector faces further deterioration (Nomura analysis). Meanwhile, the US economy, while slowing (Q4 GDP 2.6%, down from 3.5% in Q3), still has near-50-year low unemployment and a Fed that has paused rate hikes. The 10-year Treasury yield has fallen from 3.2% to 2.61%, signaling growth concerns, but no recession is imminent. Our tariff coverage ($250B of Chinese imports) vastly exceeds China's retaliation ($110B of US goods), giving us asymmetric leverage. The Huawei prosecution and Meng Wanzhou extradition (hearing underway March 6 in Vancouver) add non-tariff pressure on China's tech ambitions. China is the party under greater economic stress.

ACTION SCORE (-0.15): Despite favorable leverage, maximal escalation would be counterproductive at this moment. First, talks are actively progressing — six MOUs are being drafted on structural issues (forced tech transfer, IP, services, currency, agriculture, non-tariff barriers), and China has reportedly prepared structural concessions (NYT, Feb 21). Second, US domestic costs are real: the trade deficit has widened (soybean exports collapsed under Chinese retaliation), farmers are hurting, GDP forecasts for 2019 are being trimmed to 1.9-2.3%, and the Mercatus March 2019 report flags trade policy as one of three 'dark clouds' alongside the shutdown aftermath and Fed uncertainty. Third, the enforcement mechanism — not tariff levels — is the critical prize. Lighthizer's team wants a process allowing tariffs to snap back if China reneges; getting that structural commitment matters more than squeezing another few points of tariff pressure now. The List 3 hike from 10% to 25% was already delayed once (Feb 24); keeping it suspended as leverage while pressing on enforcement is the optimal strategy. Escalation remains available if talks stall, but premature escalation would undercut our negotiating partners (Liu He) and rally Chinese domestic nationalism.
